title: Hypergeometric face survival gives an exact expected Euler characteristic
status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: Each simplex survives exactly when all of its vertices are sampled, giving a hypergeometric inclusion probability. Linearity of expectation then yields an exact polynomial transform of the face counts, without pretending that the alternating sum recovers a barcode.
definitions: Let K be a finite abstract simplicial complex on N vertices and f_{b−1} its number of faces with b vertices.
Choose an m-element vertex subset S uniformly and let K[S] contain exactly the faces of K whose vertices lie in S.
Use ordinary Euler characteristic χ(K[S])=∑_{b≥1}(−1)^{b−1}f_{b−1}(K[S]); the empty complex has χ=0.

result.name: Exact fixed-size sampling identity
result.statement: Eχ(K[S])=∑_{b≥1}(−1)^{b−1}f_{b−1}·C(m,b)/C(N,b), with the ratio zero for b>m. For independent vertex retention probability p the corresponding formula is ∑(−1)^{b−1}f_{b−1}p^b.
result.proof: Write the random face count as a sum of indicators over the original faces. A fixed b-vertex face lies in exactly C(N−b,m−b) of the C(N,m) possible samples. Their ratio equals C(m,b)/C(N,b) by factorial cancellation. Taking expectations and the alternating sum proves the identity; independence between faces is unnecessary. Under independent retention, a face’s inclusion probability is p^b instead. For fixed b and m/N=ρ bounded away from zero, expanding the product ∏_{j=0}^{b−1}(m−j)/(N−j) gives log Π=b log ρ−(1−ρ)b(b−1)/(2ρN)+O(N^{−2}); the constant may depend on b and the lower bound on ρ. In dimension three this becomes f₀p−f₁p²+f₂p³−f₃p⁴, with the same hypergeometric replacement for fixed-size sampling. This is an exact finite identity, not an asymptotic density argument.

example.setup: Take K to be the four-cycle graph, with N=4 and four edges, and sample m=2 vertices.
example.calculation: There are six samples. Four adjacent pairs induce an edge with χ=1; two opposite pairs induce isolated vertices with χ=2. Their mean is (4+4)/6=4/3. The formula gives 4·(2/4)−4·(1/6)=4/3. For m=3 each sample is a three-vertex path and χ=1.
example.conclusion: The full finite distribution checks the expectation and reveals the variability hidden by its mean.

summary: A four-cycle with independent vertex arrival times gives a complete random persistence interval. The example distinguishes a necessary support-survival law from claims about arbitrary cycle detection, where alternative representatives and earlier fillings change the answer.
definitions: Give each vertex of a four-cycle an independent Uniform[0,1] birth time U_i. An edge enters when both its endpoints have arrived.

title: Weighted sampling replaces hypergeometric ratios by symmetric polynomials
status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: A product-weight distribution on subsets has an elementary-symmetric normalizer. This yields an exact inclusion law and a dynamic program for expected Euler characteristic, while clarifying that different without-replacement sampling schemes need not share this law.
definitions: Choose positive vertex weights w₁,…,w_N and a size m. Give an m-element subset S probability ∏_{i∈S}w_i/e_m(w), where e_m(w)=∑_{|S|=m}∏_{i∈S}w_i.
For a fixed vertex set F of size b, let w_{Fᶜ} denote the remaining weights and w_F=∏_{i∈F}w_i.
This is a specified subset distribution, not an assertion about sequential probability-proportional-to-size draws.

result.statement: P(F⊂S)=w_F e_{m−b}(w_{Fᶜ})/e_m(w), for b≤m. Consequently expected Euler characteristic is the alternating sum of these probabilities over the faces. The e_r can be computed by E_{j,r}=E_{j−1,r}+w_jE_{j−1,r−1}.

Dividing by the original normalizer proves the formula. To derive the recurrence, split r-element subsets of the first j vertices into those omitting j and those containing it. Initialize E_{0,0}=1 and E_{0,r}=0 for r>0. Updating r in descending order uses O(m) storage and O(Nm) arithmetic operations. Equal weights give e_m=C(N,m)w^m and recover the uniform hypergeometric probability exactly.

title: Compatibility and gluing can be tested by a linear obstruction
status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: Differences prescribed on graph edges glue to vertex potentials exactly when their cycle sums vanish. This finite model gives a complete obstruction theory and clarifies when a rank-sized witness is merely linear redundancy rather than a theorem translating every mathematical branch.
definitions: Let B be the oriented incidence matrix of a connected finite graph. An edge datum a∈R^m is compatible with vertex potentials when a=Bᵀx for some x∈R^n.
A cycle vector c satisfies Bc=0. The obstruction functional is cᵀa.
For a finite collection of row vectors A_W, define r(W) as the least number of selected rows with the same row-space rank.

result.name: Cycle obstruction criterion and minimal linear witness
result.statement: The edge data glue if and only if cᵀa=0 for every cycle c. The solution is unique up to an additive constant. Moreover r(W)=rank(A_W), provided individual rows may be chosen freely.
result.proof: The orthogonal complement of im Bᵀ is ker B, since ⟨Bᵀx,c⟩=⟨x,Bc⟩. In finite-dimensional Euclidean space taking orthogonal complements again proves im Bᵀ=(ker B)⊥, giving necessity and sufficiency. If two potentials solve the equations their difference lies in ker Bᵀ, which consists of constants by connectivity. For r(W), any r selected rows have rank at most r, establishing the lower bound. A basis of the full row space can be selected from its spanning rows by Gaussian elimination, attaining the bound. This proves the source’s witness-size expression in its linear setting; nonlinear or constrained witnesses can behave differently.

example.setup: Orient a triangle as 1→2→3→1 and prescribe edge increments (2,3,−5).
example.calculation: The unique cycle sum is 2+3−5=0. Taking x₁=0 gives x₂=2 and x₃=5, and the final edge requires x₁−x₃=−5, which holds. Replacing the final datum by −4 gives cycle sum one and no global potential, although each individual edge equation has solutions. The three incidence rows have rank two, so two independent edge equations form a rank witness, but the third still supplies a consistency test on the right-hand side.
example.conclusion: Local solvability, coefficient rank and right-hand-side consistency are distinct and explicitly measurable.

title: Prefix geometry has an exact Hausdorff dimension and a carry obstruction
status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: A weighted symbolic boundary has a provable ultrametric and a computable Hausdorff dimension. Its ordinary radix-value map is continuous but identifies boundary expansions and has no uniform inverse modulus, while p-adic distance compares low-order digits under a different arithmetic convention.
definitions: Let Σ_b={0,…,b−1}^N, b≥2. For distinct sequences let ℓ(x,y) be their common-prefix length and define d(x,y)=a^{ℓ(x,y)}, with 0<a<1; d(x,x)=0.
A length-k cylinder fixes the first k digits and has diameter a^k. Use the uniform product measure, giving each cylinder mass b^{−k}.
The real radix map is π(x)=∑_{j≥1}x_jb^{−j}.

result.name: Ultrametric, dimension and failure of an inverse Lipschitz estimate
result.statement: d is an ultrametric and dim_HΣ_b=log b/log(1/a). Sequences agreeing through k digits have |π(x)−π(y)|≤b^{−k}. The map π need not be injective, and small real distance does not force a long common prefix.
result.proof: Two pairs with prefix lengths r and s force the third pair to agree through min(r,s), proving d(x,z)≤max(d(x,y),d(y,z)). Covering by all b^k cylinders gives Hausdorff s-content at most (ba^s)^k, hence the upper dimension bound. Conversely a ball of radius comparable to a^k has mass at most a constant times b^{−k}=a^{ks₀}, with s₀=log b/log(1/a). The mass-distribution inequality then bounds below the s₀-dimensional Hausdorff content, giving equality. For π, sum the largest possible tail: ∑_{j>k}(b−1)b^{−j}=b^{−k}. The familiar two expansions of a terminating radix value show noninjectivity, so a global inverse modulus is impossible.

example.setup: Use binary sequences and a=1/4.
example.calculation: The dimension is log2/log4=1/2. The sequences .1000… and .0111… both map to 1/2, despite disagreeing immediately. Replacing the latter by .011…11000… gives distinct real numbers arbitrarily close to 1/2 while their first digits still differ. By contrast, in Z₂ the numbers 1 and 1+2^k are 2^{−k} apart because their low-order digits agree.
example.conclusion: Representation geometry and arithmetic topology must be specified before prefix depth is used as a stability invariant.

summary: A stable line bundle on a smooth projective elliptic curve has a one-dimensional self-extension space. Serre duality then explains why splitting claims and vanishing mixed extensions need actual category hypotheses rather than analogy with independent simples.
definitions: Let X be a smooth connected projective complex curve of genus one, and let L be a line bundle. Its canonical bundle is trivial.
For locally free L, Ext¹_X(L,L)=H¹(X,End L)=H¹(X,O_X). A line bundle is slope-stable because it has no proper positive-rank subsheaf of smaller rank.

title: A fund target is an annuity recurrence with explicit assumptions
status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: An exact linear recurrence separates contributions, assumed returns and payouts. It turns the historical numerical target into a transparent mathematical scenario, without treating a proposed allocation or future return as established fact.
definitions: Let W_n be a fund balance after year n, W₀=0, r a constant net annual return and c a constant contribution paid at year end. Use W_{n+1}=(1+r)W_n+c.
Assume r>−1 and specify that all values are nominal. Fees, inflation and uncertain returns are absent unless introduced explicitly.
For a monthly payout D to P recipients, the annual payout is 12DP, a flow with different units from the asset stock.

result.name: Exact target and payout arithmetic
result.statement: For r≠0, W_n=c[(1+r)^n−1]/r; at r=0 it equals nc. A target T at year n requires c=Tr/[(1+r)^n−1]. A balance by itself does not determine a sustainable payout.
result.proof: Iterate the recurrence to get c∑_{j=0}^{n−1}(1+r)^j and sum the geometric series. The r→0 limit is n by the derivative of (1+r)^n. If a fixed annual payout b is also made, replace c by c−b in the same recurrence; a nonnegative nominal equilibrium under this simplified accounting needs inflow plus modeled return to cover b. For variable returns, the exact balance is a weighted sum of contributions multiplied by subsequent return products, so order and volatility matter. Neither an expected return nor a portfolio percentage makes the constant-r path certain.

example.setup: Take T=10 trillion units and n=20.
example.calculation: At r=0 the required yearly contribution is .5 trillion. At the explicitly hypothetical r=.05, it is about .302426 trillion because 1.05²⁰≈2.653298. For P=100 million, monthly D=200 costs .24 trillion annually, while D=800 costs .96 trillion. These are arithmetic flows, not forecasts of affordable distributions.
example.conclusion: The target, horizon, contribution timing and payout denominator are all visible in the calculation.

limits: This entry supplies no investment recommendation or prediction. Inflation, taxes, risk, demographics and changes in contributions can materially alter the model; historical policy targets remain proposals.
extension: Replace constant r by a stated stochastic return model, derive the distribution of terminal wealth and shortfall probability, and compare real rather than nominal targets with an explicit inflation process.

title: Changing the scalar domain changes solvability
status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: A linear Diophantine equation and a quadratic illustrate how the chosen scalar domain changes both existence and structure. The domains are connected by embeddings, but their divisibility, completeness and order properties cannot be interchanged.
definitions: Use N={1,2,…} and N₀={0,1,2,…}; this convention makes N⊂N₀⊂Z⊂Q⊂R⊂C.
For integers a,b not both zero, gcd(a,b) is their positive greatest common divisor. A Diophantine solution requires integer unknowns.
A field allows division by every nonzero element. An ordered field has an order compatible with addition and multiplication; C cannot carry such an order.

result.name: Solvability criteria and a domain boundary
result.statement: ax+by=c has an integer solution exactly when gcd(a,b) divides c. The equation x²=2 has no rational solution but has two real solutions; x²=−1 has no real solution but has solutions ±i in C.
result.proof: Every integer linear combination of a,b is divisible by their gcd, proving necessity. Euclid’s algorithm yields integers u,v with au+bv=gcd(a,b); multiply by c/gcd(a,b) for sufficiency. If x²=2 with x=r/s in lowest positive terms, r²=2s² makes r even; writing r=2k makes s even as well, contradicting coprimality. Completeness of R supplies √2, for example as the supremum of positive rationals with square below two. In an ordered field every square is nonnegative; therefore i²=−1 rules out an ordered-field structure on C extending ordinary arithmetic.

example.setup: Compare 6x+9y=3 with 6x+9y=1.
example.calculation: The first has integer solution (−1,1) because −6+9=3, and all solutions are x=−1+3t,y=1−2t for t∈Z. The second has no integer solution since three does not divide one, but has rational solution (1/6,0). Thus even an elementary equation needs its coefficient and solution domains declared.
example.conclusion: Embeddings preserve arithmetic identities while new elements can change solvability and available analytic tools.

limits: This does not classify every equation or foundational system. Complex square-root notation is multivalued unless a branch is chosen, and completeness of R is an additional property rather than a formal consequence of being a field.
extension: For a polynomial or linear system, compare solutions under field extension and integral constraints, compute exact obstruction invariants, and state which analytic arguments require completeness rather than algebra alone.

title: Prefix entropy grows by conditional information, not by metric contraction alone
status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: The chain rule bounds the information added by each digit. A deterministic prefix contraction can reduce finite-resolution entropy, while a fresh random prefix increases it, demonstrating that geometric closeness and stochastic information generation require different hypotheses.
definitions: Let X=(X₁,X₂,…) be a random sequence over b symbols and H_k=H(X₁,…,X_k), using natural logarithms.
A deterministic prefix map G(x)=0x prepends a fixed digit. In the metric a^{common-prefix length}, it contracts all distances by a.
A random prefix map instead prepends an independent uniform symbol U. Its output law includes new randomness not present in the deterministic map.

result.name: Entropy refinement law and two contrasting generators
result.statement: 0≤H_{k+1}−H_k=H(X_{k+1}|X₁,…,X_k)≤log b. For fixed-prefix G, H_k(GX)=H_{k−1}(X). For a fresh independent uniform prefix, H_k(UX)=log b+H_{k−1}(X).
result.proof: Factor a joint probability into its prefix probability and conditional next-symbol probability inside the logarithm defining Shannon entropy. Summing gives the chain rule. Conditional entropy is a probability-weighted average of entropies on at most b symbols, each between zero and log b; Jensen’s inequality proves the upper bound. For a fixed first digit there is no entropy contribution at that position and the remaining observed coordinates are the first k−1 old ones. For an independent uniform first digit, add its entropy log b by independence. The deterministic map increases pairwise common-prefix length by one, yet its finite observation reveals one fewer old coordinate. Thus the metric refinement inequality alone does not establish uniqueness generation or an entropy source.

example.setup: Let X be an independent fair binary sequence and k=4.
example.calculation: Originally H₄=4log2. Prepending zero gives H₄=3log2; prepending a fresh fair bit leaves H₄=4log2. If X is deterministic instead, the fresh-prefix operation gives H₄=log2 while the deterministic operation remains zero. These exact counts distinguish information redistribution from genuine randomization.
example.conclusion: A proposed generator must specify both its action on sequences and the source of randomness.

limits: Thermodynamic energy costs do not follow from Shannon entropy change without a physical memory model, temperature and permitted operations. Prefix contraction is not an unconditional information-production theorem.
extension: For a declared stochastic transducer, derive its entropy-rate balance and the mutual information retained about the input. Combine it with an explicit channel or thermodynamic model only after identifying discarded, stored and newly randomized degrees of freedom.

references.label: Claude Shannon, A Mathematical Theory of Communication

title: A quadratic Wasserstein proximal step has an exact pushforward solution
status: Developed mathematical treatment with explicit hypotheses, derivation and checked example
summary: A quadratic potential on probability measures admits a closed-form proximal map. Completing the square inside a coupling proves contraction exactly, providing a rigorous transport model while preserving the distinction between metric convergence and exact tower stabilization.
definitions: Let μ have finite second moment on R^d, λ>0 and τ>0. Minimize J(ν)=(λ/2)∫|x|²dν+W₂²(ν,μ)/(2τ).
W₂² is the infimum of ∫|x−y|² over couplings with x-law ν and y-law μ.
Set q=(1+λτ)⁻¹ and T(y)=qy.

result.name: Exact minimizer and contraction
result.statement: The unique minimizer is ν=T_#μ. For two input measures μ,η, their outputs satisfy W₂(T_#μ,T_#η)=qW₂(μ,η). Repeated proximal steps therefore contract at rate q^n toward δ₀.
result.proof: Combine the energy and transport cost in one joint integral. Pointwise in y, (λ/2)|x|²+|x−y|²/(2τ) equals (λ+τ⁻¹)|x−qy|²/2 plus λ|y|²/[2(1+λτ)]. The second term is fixed by μ, and the first is nonnegative, vanishing only when x=qy. The deterministic coupling therefore attains the minimum and fixes the unique output law. Scaling any coupling by q gives the upper W₂ bound. Conversely rescale an output coupling by 1/q to recover an input coupling, giving the lower bound and equality. Iteration yields q^n scaling, and W₂(q^n_#μ,δ₀)=q^n(∫|y|²dμ)^{1/2}.

example.setup: Take λ=2,τ=1/2 and μ=N(2,9) on R.
example.calculation: Then q=1/2, so one step gives N(1,9/4); n steps give N(2^{1−n},9·4^{−n}). Distance to δ₀ starts at √13 and becomes 2^{−n}√13. The contraction and all moments are exact rather than inferred from an empirical fit.
example.conclusion: A precise variational problem yields the historical contraction factor with a complete proof. In particular its contraction rate is uniform over all finite-second-moment inputs, rather than fitted to one Gaussian trajectory.

limits: This energy contains no entropy term; adding entropy changes the proximal solution. Metric contraction alone does not prove exact equality of finite prefixes, Mittag–Leffler stabilization or a vanishing derived-limit obstruction without compatible observation hypotheses.
extension: Add relative entropy and derive the corresponding JKO Euler equation, then prove a quantitative convergence theorem under explicit displacement convexity. Combine it with the observation-cell condition from the finite-resolution entry before making a tower-stability claim.
